It was the email of my dreams! It popped into my inbox a few months ago and was from someone at the ABC, saying that as part of an oral history project, Sally Sara would like to interview me about my first book, The Battle for Bennelong.

Sally Sara! I’ve listened to Radio National Breakfast every morning for years, regarding the calm, measured tones of Sally as an essential beginning to my day. I don’t live with my partner during the week – not because he’s a prisoner on weekend release, as my friends assume – but because he lives out of Sydney. Basically, I’m in a parasocial relationship with Sally, as we spend so much time together. I’m her biggest fan.

Overwhelmed with excitement, I wrote back saying I’d be delighted to contribute. Sally’s assistant wrote to me again, asking for more details. So I sat down one weekend and poured my heart out onto the page – my inspiration, research techniques, my oeuvre. Finally, someone cared about my oeuvre!

I’ve written four books – two under my own name and two as a ghostwriter – no prizes for guessing which ones made me more money. You don’t write books in Australia for profit unless you’re a fantasy author, and I’m too old to even think about people who have sex with dragons.

Writing a book, being alone in a small room with nothing but a computer and your own thoughts, is so awful that it does, temporarily, send you mad. I wrote my last book – The Teal Revolution – over winter, clad only in an unwashed Uniqlo fleece and tracksuit pants. One morning, as I was slouching out for coffee, the local church ladies mistook me for a homeless person and offered me free bread.

Journalist, author and columnist

Soon the assistant emailed me again, asking more specific questions. In my day job, I’m fairly familiar with AI writing, so I was surprised to see that these emails had slabs of AI text. Was the ABC so cash-strapped that the staff were using AI to write missives? Undeterred, I wrote back, explaining in great detail my “method” and “creative process”....
